subtopic_detail: Fluctuant lump in a breastfeeding woman whose mastitis has not settled after two days of oral antibiotics
stem:
You are the doctor in a women's health clinic seeing a woman five weeks after the birth of her first baby. She was prescribed oral flucloxacillin two days ago for a red painful right breast and has taken every dose.

Her temperature has settled but the pain has become sharply localised and she now feels a lump that was not there yesterday. The upper outer quadrant contains a 4 cm tender area that is red and shiny, and it feels fluctuant with a smooth rounded edge that does not move with the skin. Milk expressed from that breast looks normal and the baby is feeding well and gaining weight. There is no cracked nipple, no axillary lymphadenopathy and no overlying skin necrosis. An ultrasound performed this morning shows a 38 by 30 mm collection with internal debris and no solid component.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fluctuant tender 4 cm mass in the right upper outer quadrant with overlying erythema, no skin breakdown, no axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Imaging: Breast ultrasound shows a 38 by 30 mm fluid collection with internal debris and no solid component

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange ultrasound guided needle aspiration of the collection and continue antibiotics and feeding
options.rationale: Needle aspiration under ultrasound guidance drains most lactational abscesses, can be repeated, and avoids the scarring and milk fistula associated with open surgery. Feeding or expressing from the affected breast continues because milk stasis perpetuates the infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Refer her for formal incision and drainage of the breast in theatre under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Open drainage is reserved for very large collections, overlying skin necrosis or abscesses that recur after repeated aspiration, and it produces more scarring and a longer interruption to feeding. Ultrasound guided aspiration is the first line drainage method (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Change the antibiotic to oral cefalexin and review her in the clinic again in three days time
options.rationale: An established collection will not resolve with any oral antibiotic because the drug cannot penetrate pus, so changing agents simply delays drainage. A change of antibiotic is appropriate for cellulitis that is failing therapy without a collection on imaging (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Advise her to stop feeding from the affected breast and suppress lactation with cabergoline
options.rationale: Stopping drainage of the breast worsens stasis and delays resolution, and abrupt suppression is not required for a treatable infection. Suppression is considered only when a woman has decided to wean for her own reasons (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Organise mammography with core biopsy of the lesion before undertaking any drainage procedure
options.rationale: Imaging has already shown a simple collection with no solid component in a clinically typical lactational abscess, so tissue sampling is not needed first. Biopsy becomes relevant if the mass persists after drainage or has solid areas, since inflammatory breast cancer can mimic mastitis (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom).
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis progresses to abscess in a small proportion of women, most often when treatment is delayed or when milk drainage from the affected segment is incomplete. The clinical shift is from diffuse hardness and fever to a discrete fluctuant mass, and ultrasound both confirms the collection and guides drainage. Aspiration with a wide bore needle, repeated every few days if required, achieves resolution in most cases while preserving breastfeeding. Antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus continue alongside drainage, and the aspirate is sent for culture because resistant organisms are increasingly seen. Persistent masses after adequate drainage must be investigated for malignancy, as inflammatory breast cancer can present during lactation.
key_points: A fluctuant mass appearing during treated mastitis signals abscess formation
Ultrasound guided aspiration is first line drainage and may be repeated
Antibiotics alone cannot clear an established collection
Continued feeding or expressing from the affected breast aids resolution
A residual mass after drainage requires imaging and biopsy to exclude malignancy
explanation.pearls: Send the aspirated pus for culture every time, because methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus is now recovered often enough in community lactational abscesses to change the antibiotic in a meaningful minority of women.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess
Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia at twenty eight weeks in a woman who cannot tolerate any oral iron preparation
stem:
You are the registrar in the antenatal clinic reviewing a 31 year old woman at 28 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her routine bloods show a haemoglobin of 92 g/L with a ferritin of 8 micrograms/L.

She has tried three different oral iron preparations since her booking visit, including alternate day dosing, and each produced severe nausea and constipation that she could not sustain beyond a fortnight. She is tired and breathless climbing stairs but has no chest pain or palpitations. She is vegetarian, has had no bleeding in this pregnancy, and her previous birth involved a postpartum haemorrhage of 900 mL. Her mean cell volume is 76 fL and her C reactive protein is 2 mg/L. Her blood group is O positive with a negative antibody screen and there is no history of transfusion reaction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 76 fL (80-100), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), blood group O positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Prescribe a further oral iron preparation to be taken on alternate days with ascorbic acid
options.rationale: She has already failed three preparations including alternate day dosing, so a fourth trial predictably fails and wastes the weeks remaining before birth. Ascorbic acid modestly improves absorption but does nothing for the gastrointestinal intolerance that is the limiting problem (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy).

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron infusion now and recheck her haemoglobin in about four weeks
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is indicated for established iron deficiency anaemia with oral intolerance or failure, and is used from the second trimester onwards with a haemoglobin response over two to four weeks. Repleting stores before birth also lowers the transfusion risk that her previous postpartum haemorrhage makes relevant (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells to correct the anaemia in advance of her birth
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia with haemodynamic compromise or active bleeding, and exposes her to alloimmunisation that could affect a future pregnancy. She has weeks available in which iron replacement can raise the haemoglobin instead (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.text: Start vitamin B12 and folate supplementation and repeat the full blood examination in six weeks
options.rationale: Her low mean cell volume with a ferritin of 8 micrograms/L identifies iron deficiency rather than a megaloblastic process, which would raise the cell volume instead. B12 assessment is worth adding in a long standing vegan diet but does not treat the deficiency present (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy).

options.text: Investigate for a haemoglobinopathy with electrophoresis before committing her to any iron therapy
options.rationale: A ferritin of 8 micrograms/L with a normal C reactive protein already establishes iron deficiency as the cause of the microcytosis, and iron studies must be interpreted before electrophoresis because deficiency itself distorts the haemoglobin A2 fraction. Screening is prompted by microcytosis with normal iron stores (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Iron requirements roughly triple across pregnancy and dietary intake rarely meets them, so iron deficiency is the commonest medical problem of the antenatal period and is associated with preterm birth, low birthweight and postpartum depression. Ferritin is the most useful single test but is an acute phase reactant, which is why a normal C reactive protein matters when interpreting a low value. Oral iron remains first line and alternate day dosing improves absorption by reducing hepcidin induction, but intolerance is common. Intravenous preparations replete stores in a single visit and are used in the second and third trimesters when oral therapy fails, is not tolerated, or when birth is too close for oral therapy to work. Adequate stores before birth reduce the likelihood of transfusion when postpartum haemorrhage occurs.
key_points: Ferritin below 30 micrograms/L indicates deficiency, and below 15 micrograms/L indicates absent stores
Intravenous iron is indicated for oral intolerance, oral failure, or late gestation presentation
Alternate day oral dosing improves fractional absorption by limiting hepcidin rise
Transfusion is for haemodynamic compromise or active bleeding, not for a number alone
Interpret haemoglobinopathy screening only after iron status is known
explanation.pearls: Expect a haemoglobin rise of about 20 g/L in two to four weeks after intravenous iron, and recheck ferritin no sooner than four weeks because the infused iron keeps the level artificially high before then.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Household exposure to chickenpox at sixteen weeks in a woman with negative varicella serology
stem:
You are the general practitioner telephoned by a 29 year old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant. Her four year old nephew stayed at her house the night before last and developed a vesicular rash yesterday morning, which his own doctor has diagnosed as chickenpox.

She played with him for several hours on both days. She has no rash, no fever and no respiratory symptoms today, and feels entirely well. She does not recall having chickenpox and was not vaccinated as a child. Her booking bloods, taken six weeks ago, include a varicella zoster immunoglobulin G that was reported as not detected. She has no immunosuppressive illness, takes no corticosteroids, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated so far. It is currently 30 hours since her last contact with the child.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No rash, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Booking varicella zoster immunoglobulin G not detected, full blood examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give her the varicella vaccine today and arrange a second dose in four weeks as planned
options.rationale: Varicella vaccine is a live attenuated preparation and is contraindicated during pregnancy, so it cannot be used for post exposure protection here. Vaccination is offered instead in the postpartum period before discharge (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Reassure her that maternal antibody will protect the pregnancy and review her only if a rash appears
options.rationale: Her booking serology shows she has no protective antibody, which is precisely why she is at risk of severe varicella pneumonitis and of transmitting infection to the fetus. Reassurance without action would be appropriate only if immunoglobulin G had been detected (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Arrange zoster immunoglobulin as soon as possible and advise her to report any rash immediately
options.rationale: A seronegative pregnant woman with significant exposure should receive zoster immunoglobulin, ideally within 96 hours and up to ten days after contact, to attenuate maternal disease. Prompt reporting of a rash then allows oral aciclovir to be started within 24 hours of its onset (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Commence oral aciclovir immediately at treatment dose and continue it for the next seven days
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy is started when a rash appears rather than at the point of exposure, since it is most effective within 24 hours of the first vesicles. Presumptive antiviral use is not the recommended post exposure strategy in a seronegative pregnant contact (Source: RANZCOG: Varicella in pregnancy).

options.text: Organise amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction testing to assess the risk to the fetus
options.rationale: Invasive testing is not indicated in an exposed woman who has not developed infection, and it carries a procedure related loss risk. It is considered only after confirmed maternal varicella when detailed ultrasound raises concern about fetal involvement (Source: RANZCOG: Varicella in pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Varicella in pregnancy is dangerous for both mother and fetus, with maternal pneumonitis carrying substantial mortality and first and early second trimester infection risking congenital varicella syndrome. Most Australian adults are immune, so the first step after an exposure is to establish serostatus, and a booking result showing no detectable immunoglobulin G answers that immediately. Seronegative women with significant exposure receive zoster immunoglobulin, which attenuates rather than prevents infection, and the window extends to ten days although earlier administration works better. If a rash develops, oral aciclovir started within 24 hours reduces the duration and severity of maternal illness. Infection between 28 weeks and delivery raises the separate problem of neonatal varicella, which requires immunoglobulin for the newborn.
key_points: Live vaccines including varicella are contraindicated in pregnancy
Zoster immunoglobulin is given to seronegative pregnant contacts, ideally within 96 hours and up to ten days
Aciclovir is for treatment once a rash appears, started within 24 hours of the first vesicles
Congenital varicella syndrome risk is highest with infection before 20 weeks and is around 1 to 2 per cent
Maternal infection from five days before to two days after birth requires immunoglobulin for the neonate
explanation.pearls: Offer varicella vaccination postpartum to any woman found seronegative at booking, giving the first dose before hospital discharge because the return rate for a deferred first dose is poor and breastfeeding is not a contraindication.

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis three months after birth in a breastfeeding woman with a painless gland
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a woman three months after the birth of her second child. She reports palpitations, sweating and irritability for the past three weeks and has lost 4 kg despite eating well.

She is fully breastfeeding. Her thyroid is not enlarged, not nodular and not tender, and she has no eye signs, no pretibial change and no thyroid bruit. She had a similar episode after her first birth that settled without treatment, though she then felt sluggish and cold for several months. Her thyroid stimulating hormone is less than 0.01 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 34 pmol/L. Thyroid receptor antibodies are negative and thyroid peroxidase antibodies are strongly positive. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 12 mm per hour.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 per minute and regular, blood pressure 128/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, warm peripheries, thyroid not palpable and non tender, no eye signs
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 34 pmol/L (10-20), thyroid receptor antibodies negative, thyroid peroxidase antibodies strongly positive, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 12 mm per hour (less than 20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start carbimazole and titrate the dose against her thyroid function tests every four weeks
options.rationale: Thionamides block synthesis of new hormone and have no effect on hormone leaking from an inflamed gland, so they do not shorten this illness. They are the treatment when receptor antibodies are positive and the gland is overproducing (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Prescribe propranolol for symptom control and recheck her thyroid function in four to six weeks
options.rationale: A painless destructive thyroiditis after birth with negative receptor antibodies is self limiting, so a beta blocker compatible with breastfeeding covers the symptomatic phase while the process runs its course. Repeat testing detects the hypothyroid phase that follows in a substantial proportion of women (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Refer her for radioactive iodine uptake scanning to establish the cause of her thyrotoxicosis
options.rationale: Radioisotope studies require interruption of breastfeeding and are not needed when negative receptor antibodies, a non tender gland and the postpartum timing already indicate a destructive process. Uptake scanning is reserved for cases where the distinction from Graves disease remains genuinely unclear and feeding has ceased (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Begin levothyroxine now in anticipation of the hypothyroid phase that typically develops later
options.rationale: Giving thyroid hormone during a thyrotoxic phase compounds the excess and worsens her symptoms, and not every woman progresses to a hypothyroid phase. Replacement is started when the hypothyroid phase is symptomatic or biochemically marked (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Commence prednisolone at an anti inflammatory dose and taper it over the following four weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are used for painful subacute thyroiditis where inflammation causes significant neck pain, and her gland is not tender with a normal sedimentation rate. Steroid exposure adds risk without changing the course of the painless postpartum form (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis is an autoimmune destructive process affecting a few per cent of women in the year after birth, and it classically runs through a thyrotoxic phase at two to six months, a hypothyroid phase, and then recovery. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are usually positive and predict both recurrence in later pregnancies and long term hypothyroidism. The key clinical task is separating it from Graves disease, since the treatments differ entirely, and negative receptor antibodies with a non tender impalpable gland make destruction far more likely. Management is symptomatic with a beta blocker in the thyrotoxic phase and levothyroxine if the hypothyroid phase is symptomatic. Around one in five affected women develop permanent hypothyroidism, so annual thyroid function testing is recommended thereafter.
key_points: Postpartum thyroiditis is destructive, so thionamides are ineffective
Negative receptor antibodies with a non tender gland distinguish it from Graves disease
Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies predict recurrence and later permanent hypothyroidism
Propranolol is compatible with breastfeeding and covers the thyrotoxic phase
Radioisotope uptake studies require interruption of breastfeeding and are rarely needed
explanation.pearls: Check thyroid function annually after an episode, because roughly 20 per cent of women develop permanent hypothyroidism within a few years and the risk is highest in those with strongly positive peroxidase antibodies.

subtopic_detail: Urinary leakage with coughing and exercise in a parous woman with a normal post void residual
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46 year old woman who leaks urine when she coughs, sneezes or plays netball. It began after her third vaginal birth and has worsened over two years to the point where she wears a pad on training days.

She empties her bladder about six times a day and once at night, and does not leak on the way to the toilet or when she hears running water. She has no dysuria, no haematuria and no pelvic pain. Examination shows a well oestrogenised vagina, no prolapse beyond the hymen, and leakage of urine from the urethra when she coughs with a comfortably full bladder. Her bladder scan afterwards shows a post void residual of 20 mL. Urine dipstick is negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood, and her body mass index is 31 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Leakage from the urethra on coughing with a full bladder, no prolapse beyond the hymen, well oestrogenised vaginal epithelium
data_table.Investigations: Post void residual 20 mL, urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood, bladder diary shows six voids per day and one at night

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Prescribe an anticholinergic bladder relaxant and review her symptom diary in three months
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic drugs treat detrusor overactivity, which produces urgency and leakage on the way to the toilet rather than leakage synchronous with a cough. Her diary and provocation findings do not support that mechanism (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women).

options.text: Refer her for urodynamic studies before any conservative treatment is offered to her
options.rationale: Urodynamics is reserved for mixed or unclear symptoms, prior failed surgery, or before an operation is planned, and it does not change the initial conservative plan. Her history and demonstrated leakage on coughing are sufficient for a working diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women).

options.text: Arrange supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist for at least three months
options.rationale: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for a minimum of three months is the first line treatment for stress incontinence and cures or improves symptoms in most women, with supervision producing substantially better results than a handout. Weight reduction and modification of fluid habits are addressed alongside it (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women).
source_refs: Continence Foundation of Australia: Clinical guidance

options.text: Refer her to a gynaecologist for a midurethral sling procedure to correct the urethral support
options.rationale: Surgery is considered only after an adequate trial of supervised conservative therapy has failed, and it requires detailed counselling about mesh related risks. Proceeding directly to operation bypasses a treatment that resolves symptoms for many women (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women).

options.text: Commence vaginal oestrogen cream three nights a week and reassess her leakage after two months
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen helps urogenital atrophy in the postmenopausal woman, and her epithelium is well oestrogenised with regular cycles. It has little effect on the sphincteric mechanism responsible for leakage on effort (Source: Continence Foundation of Australia: Clinical guidance).
source_refs: Continence Foundation of Australia: Clinical guidance

explanation.summary: Urinary incontinence in women is separated clinically into stress, urgency and mixed types, and this distinction determines the entire management pathway. Leakage that occurs simultaneously with a rise in intra abdominal pressure, without urgency and with a normal post void residual, indicates a sphincteric or support problem rather than detrusor overactivity. A bladder diary, urinalysis to exclude infection, and a post void residual are the basic assessment, and demonstrating leakage on coughing supports the diagnosis without urodynamics. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months is first line and is more effective than unsupervised exercises, with weight loss adding benefit in women with a raised body mass index. Surgery and continence pessaries are options after conservative therapy fails, and mesh procedures require explicit counselling in Australia.
key_points: Leakage synchronous with coughing and no urgency indicates stress incontinence
Basic assessment is a bladder diary, urinalysis and post void residual
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for three months or more is first line
Urodynamics is indicated for mixed or unclear pictures, or before planned surgery
Antimuscarinic drugs and vaginal oestrogen address different mechanisms and will not help here
explanation.pearls: Weight loss of 5 to 10 per cent reduces stress incontinence episodes by roughly half in women with a raised body mass index, which makes it worth negotiating alongside the physiotherapy referral rather than after it.

sources.label: Continence Foundation of Australia: Clinical guidance
